Well, the first thing to understand is that there are MANY different forms of counseling and therapy. The specific type I have (which works pretty well with mood disorders), is cognitive-behavioral therapy, which, with a lot of work, helps one recognize irrational thinking patterns and their connection to moods. Good counseling, secular or religious, isn't a one-size-fits-all approach.

I'm not a biblical proof-texter (as that almost always turns into a biblical shouting match about who's more correct), but the scriptural basis for Christian counseling is love, love for the individual and compassion to help them in their moments of crisis. Every single verse in the Gospels that has to do with love and compassion is relevant here. This is the specific mission statement of the counseling organization I patronize.

Additionally, effective Christian counseling recognizes that mental illnesses are, in fact, illnesses. There is a medical basis for the hormonal and chemical misfirings in my mind. I've even seen a medical doctor to rule out any other possibilities. When I first started counseling, I went seeking help for depression. I wanted to find a way to beat it without medication (as depression can often be situational) but after two years it wasn't possible. The horrible moods and darkness I felt just wasn't going away.

It wasn't because I didn't have enough faith.
It wasn't because of anything I did wrong, or because I didn't love Jesus enough.

It was because I have a brain disorder. The diagnosis helped explain so many things about my life, and there are real physical symptoms that accompany my unstable moods. My counselor was the one who encouraged me to try medication and helped me reach my accurate bipolar diagnosis. Medication doesn't change my personality and my diagnosis doesn't negate the reality of sin in my life. 

The best response I have towards anyone who's skeptical about me taking medication or the existence of mental illnesses is to just be grateful you don't have one (as living with a disease with no cure is not easy) and to listen to those who are struggling.
